title: Non-blocking follow-ups from backend-profit-target-weekly-channel-followups PR #223 review
description: Non-blocking findings from pr-reviewer's full review of PR #223 (backend-profit-target-weekly-channel-followups, the check_profit_target_wording.py guard script), recorded here per CLAUDE.md's convention so they aren't lost once the PR merges. All six were verified as real, demonstrated gaps in the guard's own robustness (confirmed by directly constructing inputs and running the affected functions), not currently-live false positives/negatives against the real repo tree -- and critically, none of them defeat the guard's actual protection for the 8 known regression-prone files: the per-file positive check (check_known_files_mention_weekly) operates on whole-file text at the character-window level, not per physical line, so it independently still catches a reversion in any of those 8 files even where the repo-wide negative check's line-based scanning is fooled (verified directly by reverting schemas.py's `source` field to the old stale wording, wrapped across lines matching the file's own dominant style for long Field descriptions elsewhere -- the negative check missed it, the positive check still caught it). That's why these are follow-ups rather than blocking findings.

checklist.step: check_banned_patterns() scans each physical line independently (text.splitlines()), so it misses a banned phrase split across two source lines by Python implicit string concatenation -- a style already used throughout backend/app/api/schemas.py's own IndicatorsOut field descriptions (ATR, ADX, +DI/-DI, channel_upper/channel_lower, RSI all wrap this way), just not (currently) ProfitTargetOut's own fields. Verified directly: a description=("...today's "\n    "Autoenvelope/channel height...") input produces zero violations from check_banned_patterns(). This only matters for a brand-new file outside the 8-file known-locations list (the known 8 are independently protected by the positive per-file check regardless of line-wrapping, verified directly) -- worth having the negative check join adjacent lines (or scan the whole file text with re.DOTALL/single-string search) before matching, so its own docstring's 'anywhere in the repo, including a brand-new file' claim actually holds.

_WEEKLY_RE = re.compile(r'\bweek(ly)?\b') doesn't match the plural 'weeks' on its own (\b right after the non-'ly' branch fails since 'weeks' has no boundary between 'week' and the following 's') -- verified directly: _WEEKLY_RE.search('100 weeks') is None while _WEEKLY_RE.search('100 weekly') matches. Currently harmless since every real occurrence in the repo pairs 'weeks' with 'weekly' nearby, but a future, fully-correct edit phrasing the warm-up window as e.g. '~100 weeks of price history' without the adjective 'weekly' anywhere nearby would be wrongly flagged as a stale-daily-channel regression by check_known_files_mention_weekly. Fix the regex to r'\bweeks?(ly)?\b' (or equivalent) so the plural noun form is recognized on its own.

_iter_scanned_files() calls REPO_ROOT.rglob('*') over the entire repo tree and only filters out node_modules/.venv/.git/dist/build/coverage/etc. after full enumeration, rather than pruning those directories during traversal (e.g. an os.walk with dirnames[:] = [d for d in dirnames if d not in _EXCLUDED_DIR_NAMES]). Since this script now runs as static-verify's own step 5 -- which pr-reviewer and task-qa-reviewer both run unconditionally on every task -- this wasted walk over tens of thousands of node_modules/.venv/.git files repeats on every PR review and QA pass and will only get slower as those directories grow.

_PROFIT_TARGET_CONTEXT_RE's `profit[\s_]target` alternative doesn't match the hyphenated form 'profit-target' -- the literal text of methodologyContent.ts's own start_anchor (id: 'profit-target'). Verified directly: the id text alone doesn't match. In practice the check currently still passes because the same entry's `name` field ('Profit Target (+ reward:risk ratio)') independently matches the space-separated form -- a genuine structural field of the entry, not throwaway incidental prose, so the practical fragility is lower than it first appears, but it's still an unnecessary gap: add a hyphenated alternative (`profit[\s_-]target`) so the anchor's own id text is self-sufficient context, not reliant on a second field happening to also mention it.

_extract_region() silently falls back to scanning to the end of the file when end_anchor fails to match, with no violation/warning emitted -- asymmetric with the explicit 'this guard's start anchor no longer matches -- update...' violation raised when start_anchor fails. If a known file's structure changes so the end anchor stops matching (e.g. profitTargetHelp becomes the last export in a metricHelpContent.ts, or profit-target becomes the last id: entry in methodologyContent.ts), the scanned region would silently balloon to include unrelated trailing content (e.g. the genuinely-different DAILY trade-grading description) with no signal to a maintainer that the anchor needs updating -- worth emitting the same kind of 'anchor no longer scoping correctly, update this guard' violation in that case too, for symmetry with the start-anchor check.

scripts/check_profit_target_wording.py has one ruff finding (SIM103: `_should_scan_for_banned_patterns` could return `not _is_test_file(path)` directly instead of the trailing if/return). Not part of the enforced backend `ruff check app/` gate (scripts/ at the repo root is out of scope, same precedent as scripts/validate_tasks.py) so non-blocking, but scripts/validate_tasks.py itself -- the sibling script this one explicitly mirrors -- is fully ruff-clean, so this is a small, easy inconsistency worth tidying up to match.

decisions.decision: Fixed check_banned_patterns()'s cross-line-concatenation blind spot by recognizing Python's own implicit-string-concatenation syntax specifically (a regex matching `quote, whitespace spanning a newline, matching quote` and dropping just the quote pair, preserving every newline) rather than switching to a whole-file re.DOTALL scan or blanket whitespace-collapsing normalization.
decisions.rationale: A whole-file re.DOTALL/single-string search (the alternative floated in the checklist item itself) would also match a banned phrase split across two genuinely unrelated lines/paragraphs that just happen to have the right words in the right order with nothing else between -- a broader match surface than the bug class this guard exists for, and it would make every violation's line-number reporting harder (a match spanning many lines has no single obvious 'the' line to report). Targeting the specific implicit-concatenation syntax keeps the fix narrow to the actual reported gap (schemas.py's own Field description wrapping style) while leaving every other newline in a file inert to the banned-pattern regexes, exactly as before. It also preserves exact line-number reporting for free, since only quote characters are removed, not newlines -- a plain `joined_text.count("\n", 0, match.start())` still maps correctly back to the original file's physical lines.

decisions.decision: On a failed end_anchor (checklist item 5), emit a violation but still fall back to scanning from the start anchor to end of file, rather than skipping the file's positive check entirely the way a failed start_anchor does.
decisions.rationale: A failed start_anchor means there is no valid region at all to scan, so skipping is the only option. A failed end_anchor still leaves a well-defined region start; the fallback-to-end-of-file region is a superset that still legitimately contains the real profit-target description (just with extra, possibly-unrelated trailing content risked), so scanning it can still catch a real regression even while the guard's own anchor needs a maintainer's attention -- silently disabling the positive check entirely on a stale end_anchor would be a worse outcome than an occasional extra false positive from bleeding into trailing content.

decisions.decision: Refactored _iter_scanned_files() to os.walk with dirnames[:] pruning (checklist item 3) but left the now-redundant _EXCLUDED_DIR_NAMES membership check inside _should_scan_for_banned_patterns() in place, as a defense-in-depth safety net for any future caller of that predicate outside the pruned os.walk loop, with a comment noting the redundancy.
decisions.rationale: Removing it would save a negligible amount of work per call and add a hidden coupling: _should_scan_for_banned_patterns() would only be a correct 'should this file be scanned' predicate when called from inside _iter_scanned_files()'s own pruned walk, silently wrong if called on an arbitrary path from anywhere else. Verified the traversal refactor is fully behavior-preserving by diffing the real repo's scanned-file set (217 files, byte-for-byte identical sorted path list) between the pre-change rglob-based implementation and the new os.walk-based one.

decisions.decision: Fixed PR #226's needs_work finding (the implicit-concatenation join false-flagging unrelated quoted prose/code) by (a) restricting `_join_implicit_string_concatenation` to `.py` files only in `check_banned_patterns`, and (b) rewriting the join itself to use the stdlib `tokenize` module instead of a bare regex: it now walks the real token stream and only merges two `STRING` tokens that are adjacent with nothing but `COMMENT`/`NL`/indentation tokens between them. This is the correct scoping because Python's grammar only allows two string literals to be adjacent tokens across a physical line break (as opposed to two separate statements) when they sit inside an open bracket or a backslash continuation -- outside of one, the tokenizer emits a logical-line-ending `NEWLINE` token between them instead of the non-logical `NL` used inside brackets, and a `NEWLINE` now always breaks the join.
decisions.rationale: Rejected two narrower regex patches: (1) just adding a same-quote-character check with a bracket-depth counter re-implemented by hand -- this duplicates exactly what CPython's own tokenizer already gets right (string prefixes, escaped quotes, triple-quotes, nested brackets inside strings) and risks its own new edge-case bugs; `tokenize` is stdlib (no new dependency, consistent with this script's stdlib-only philosophy) and is definitionally correct for 'is this genuine Python implicit string concatenation'. (2) Restricting to `.py` files alone without the tokenize rewrite -- this would still have false-flagged the reviewer's second repro (two unrelated bare string-literal statements in a `.py` file), since the old regex only checked for matching quote characters, not real token adjacency. Verified directly: reproduced both of the reviewer's false-positive repros (the .md two-unrelated-sentences case and the .py two-unrelated-bare-statements case) against the pre-fix code, confirmed both are now silent (no violations) against the post-fix code, and confirmed the original checklist item 1 case (schemas.py's own Field description implicit-concatenation wrapping style) is still correctly flagged. Added two new regression tests (`test_unrelated_quoted_sentences_across_a_line_break_in_md_are_not_flagged`, `test_unrelated_bare_string_statements_in_py_are_not_flagged`) alongside the pre-existing real-implicit-concatenation regression test so all three stay pinned going forward.

comments.summary: BLOCKING (round 3): task-worker's fix for the round-2 finding (join not scoped to real Python syntax) is itself confirmed correct in isolation -- both original false-positive repros (.md unrelated quoted sentences, .py unrelated bare string statements) are verified silent against the fixed code, and the original real case (schemas.py-style Field-description wrapping) is verified still caught, and the tokenize-based grammar logic (NEWLINE breaks the join, backslash-continuation outside brackets still joins, a closed-bracket-then-new-statement resets adjacency) checks out directly against CPython's own tokenizer. However, the fix's supporting rewrite of check_banned_patterns() from a per-physical-line loop to pattern.finditer(joined) over the WHOLE file text reintroduces a false-positive class broader than the one being fixed, and it applies to every scanned file type, not just .py: _BANNED_PATTERNS's regexes use \s+ (which matches real newlines under default re semantics), and joined == text unchanged for every non-.py file (and even for a .py file where no join was found), so a banned phrase split across an ORDINARY, unrelated line break -- with zero string-literal adjacency and no tokenize logic involved at all -- is now falsely flagged. Verified directly with three reproductions requiring no Python-string-concatenation syntax whatsoever: a .md file ('It happened that day's\nAutoenvelope reading looked odd.'), a .ts file ('The analyst said today's\nAutoenvelope feature shipped fine.'), and a .py file containing a single ordinary (non-implicit-concatenated) docstring wrapping the same way -- all three flagged on the current branch. Confirmed this is a genuine regression, not pre-existing: the identical .md repro produces zero violations against main (checked via git worktree). Since this script runs unconditionally on every future PR's static-verify pass, this reopens the same category of risk the round-2 review already flagged as blocking, just via a different code path (whole-text \s+ matching) than the one that was actually scoped down (the join itself).

BLOCKING (round 3): _join_implicit_string_concatenation's replacement span `(prev_end_offset - 1, cur_start_offset + 1)` deletes everything from the previous string's closing quote through the next string's opening quote inclusive -- this removes the newline (and any indentation/comments) between the two literals, not just the two quote characters, directly contradicting the function's own docstring ('preserving every other character -- including every newline -- exactly') and the PR's decision-record claim that 'a plain joined_text.count("\\n", 0, match.start()) still maps correctly back to the original file's physical lines.' Verified directly: a 7-line file with an implicit-concatenation join on lines 3-4 and a second, unrelated real violation on line 7 gets that second violation misreported as line 6 -- the join silently collapses a physical line, shifting every subsequent line number in the file by one. Doesn't cause a missed/false detection on its own, but actively misreports where a violation is, undermining the tool's core purpose (point a maintainer at the right line) and contradicting what the PR's own decision record claims was verified.

Non-blocking (carried forward, already tracked): a banned-phrase violation caught via the implicit-string-concatenation join has its printed 'found' text excerpt missing a boundary quote character -- cosmetic diagnostic-clarity nit only.

Non-blocking (carried forward, wording now stale): the already-filed follow-up task item about _STRING_CONCAT_JOIN_RE's same-quote-character limitation refers to a regex constant this PR's tokenize rewrite removed; the underlying gap (mixed-quote implicit concatenation not recognized) still exists conceptually in the new code (prev_string_token.string[-1:] == tok.string[:1] still requires matching quote chars), just under a different implementation -- the next worker picking up that follow-up item should update its wording to reference the current code.
Non-blocking (carried forward, already tracked): ruff still reports SIM110 on _is_excluded_path (pre-existing, not introduced by this PR).

review.notes: Round 3 of review on this same PR (round 1: premature accept, corrected same-session to needs_work over an unscoped join false-positive; round 2 was that correction; this is the re-review of task-worker's fix for round 2's finding). Verified all of task-worker's round-2 fix claims directly and independently: both original false-positive repros are confirmed silent post-fix, the original real case is confirmed still caught, and the tokenize-based approach's grammar logic was sanity-checked against CPython's own tokenizer (NEWLINE breaks the join; backslash-continuation outside brackets still joins correctly since no NEWLINE/NL separates the two STRING tokens; a closed-bracket-then-new-statement sequence correctly resets adjacency) rather than just trusting the fix's own description. All suites pass clean (scripts/tests: 48/48; backend pytest --cov=app --cov-fail-under=90: 1109 passed, 99.95% coverage; frontend vitest --coverage: all green, 99%+ across metrics; backend ruff/mypy clean, frontend eslint/tsc clean, ruff clean on the two changed script files; real guard run against the repo stays clean). However, going beyond just re-checking the claimed fix, direct testing of the supporting check_banned_patterns() rewrite (per-line loop -> whole-text finditer) surfaced two new, independently-reproduced blocking bugs neither task-worker's report nor the new regression tests exercise: (1) the whole-text \s+ matching now false-flags ordinary unrelated prose split across a line break in ANY scanned file type, confirmed as a genuine regression against main via a git worktree comparison; (2) the join's replacement span removes newlines it claims to preserve, silently miscounting line numbers for any content reported after a join in the same file, confirmed with a direct multi-line repro. Both undermine the round-2 fix's own stated design goals. Not UI-facing (scripts/ + docs/tasks/ only) so browser walkthrough/e2e suite skipped explicitly. area is backend/signals (inherited) but this diff touches no app/signals or app/portfolio code, so the Elder-methodology checklist doesn't apply. No API/schema changes, so no OpenAPI snapshot concern. No new module/dependency/layer (stdlib os/io/tokenize only) so no architecture-review needed. The pre-existing non-blocking findings remain filed as checklist items on backend-profit-target-weekly-channel-followups-followups-followups; no new non-blocking findings this round beyond noting that follow-up task's _STRING_CONCAT_JOIN_RE item now references a removed identifier (see comments above) -- left as-is for the next worker to update rather than editing that task from a reviewer pass.
